n: Hannah's prayer becomes a song of joy. A raised “horn” pictures an animal lifting its head in strength — God has restored her dignity and given her victory over those who mocked her.

f.g: “Horn” is a symbol of strength and honor.

f.w: My heart rejoiceth in the LORD
f.g: Mary's song in Luke 1 closely echoes Hannah's song.

n: Hannah praises God as uniquely holy and as a solid “rock” — dependable, unchanging protection. Nothing compares to Him.
She warns the proud to stop boasting, because God knows everything and weighs every action. People cannot fool Him.
A theme of reversal begins: God breaks the weapons of the strong and gives strength to those who were stumbling.

f.g: Strength wrapped around them like a belt.

n: More reversals: the well-fed must work for food while the hungry are satisfied; the barren woman has many children while the mother of many grows weak. Hannah sees her own story in God's pattern.

f.g: “Seven” symbolizes completeness — a full, blessed family.

n: God has power over life and death. Bringing people down to the grave and up again hints at His power to raise the dead.

f.w: The LORD killeth, and maketh alive

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the realm of the dead.

n: Poverty and riches, humility and honor are all in God's hands. Hebrew poetry repeats ideas in parallel pairs to emphasize them.

f.w: he bringeth low, and lifteth up

n: God lifts the poorest people from the dust and the garbage heap to sit with princes. The Creator who set the world on its foundations can surely reverse human fortunes.

f.g: a trash or ash heap outside the town, where outcasts and beggars sat.

f.w: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust

n: God protects the steps of His faithful followers, but the wicked will be silenced. Victory comes from the Lord, not human strength.

f.w: by strength shall no man prevail

n: The song ends with a prophecy of a king and an “anointed” one — remarkable since Israel had no king yet. It looks ahead to David and ultimately to Jesus, the Messiah (“Anointed One”).

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ, from which “Messiah” comes; Greek Christos (Christ).

f.w: the LORD shall judge the ends of the earth

n: Elkanah returns home, and young Samuel stays at Shiloh, serving the Lord under Eli's supervision.
In stark contrast, Eli's sons are worthless men who do not truly know the Lord, even though they are priests.
The narrator describes how the priests' servants operated. While the sacrifice meat was boiling, a servant would come with a three-pronged fork.
Whatever the fork pulled up, the priest kept. This grabbing ignored the specific portions God assigned to priests.
Worse, they demanded raw meat before the fat was burned to the Lord. The fat was God's portion and had to be offered first; they put themselves ahead of God.
If a worshipper asked them to wait until the fat was offered, the servant threatened to take the meat by force. Sacred worship became bullying.
Their sin was very serious because it made people despise the Lord's offerings. Leaders who abuse sacred trust damage others' faith.
Meanwhile the boy Samuel faithfully serves the Lord, wearing a simple linen ephod, a priestly garment. The contrast between him and Eli's sons runs through this chapter.

f.g: A simple apron-like garment worn by those serving at the sanctuary.

n: Each year Hannah makes Samuel a new little robe and brings it on their visit. This tender detail shows her continuing love for the son she gave to the Lord.
Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah, asking the Lord to give them more children in return for the son they gave to Him.

f.g: Wordplay on Samuel's name and Hannah's “asking”.

n: The Lord blesses Hannah with three more sons and two daughters. Samuel continues growing up in the Lord's presence.
Old Eli hears how his sons are abusing Israel, including sexual immorality with women serving at the tabernacle entrance — a desecration of holy ground.
Eli confronts his sons, asking why they behave this way when everyone is talking about it.
Eli tells them the reports are bad and that they are leading the Lord's people into sin. His words are correct, but he takes no real action to stop them.
Eli warns that when someone sins against God Himself, no one can plead for them. His sons ignore him; they are past the point of repentance and judgment is coming.

f.g: Who can intercede or plead on his behalf?

n: Samuel keeps growing and is favored by both God and people. Luke uses almost the same words about the young Jesus.

f.w: in favour both with the LORD, and also with men

n: An unnamed prophet comes to Eli with a message from the Lord, recalling how God revealed Himself to Eli's ancestors (Aaron's family) in Egypt.

f.g: a common title for a prophet

n: God reminds Eli of the great privilege He gave his family: chosen above all the tribes to serve as priests at His altar, wear the ephod, and receive the offerings.
So why do they treat God's sacrifices with contempt? God says Eli honored his sons above Him, letting them — and himself — grow fat on the best offerings.

f.g: treat with scorn, as a stubborn animal kicks

n: God had promised Eli's family a lasting priesthood, but promises depend on faithfulness. A key principle: those who honor God, He will honor; those who despise Him will be little regarded.

f.w: them that honour me I will honour

n: God announces that He will cut off the strength of Eli's family; its men will die young.
Eli will see distress in God's dwelling place even when Israel prospers, and his family will never have elderly members. The ark's capture and later disasters fulfill this.

f.g: The Hebrew may also mean “distress” in the sanctuary.

n: Those descendants who remain in priestly service will bring Eli grief, and many will die in their prime. Later, Saul's massacre of the priests at Nob fulfills part of this.

f.w: in the flower of their age

n: A sign will confirm the prophecy: both of Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will die on the same day.

f.w: in one day they shall die both of them

n: God will raise up a faithful priest whose family will endure and serve His anointed king. This was fulfilled in part by Samuel and especially by Zadok under Solomon.
Eli's surviving descendants will be reduced to begging for any priestly job just to eat — a humiliating reversal for a family that once grew fat on stolen offerings.
